title: How to program evolving rep ranges
summary: He explains how to fit evolving rep ranges into a program: choose movements first, then assign each lift a range and think through how they interact across the day, week and block. He prefers mixing intensity and volume within each day and favours body part splits.
claims: Do not build a whole program around a single rep range such as everything at 4 sets of 8-12; the range of volume and intensity manipulation is too narrow and will eventually fail you
Program order: pick movements, make sure they work together and stay specific, then assign each an evolving rep range while considering interactions across the day, week and 15-day block
Writing a program should take a long time with reflection periods; changes once you run it must be rare and tiny, never a big tonnage shift
Assign ranges per lift depending on whether it is strength work or a priority you want to progress fast on, such as a weak point
A beta test is fine; start with a wider range, such as close grip bench 6-12, and narrow to 6-10 if needed, because shrinking a range is safer than expanding it into other work
A rep range that works on a 6-day push/pull/legs will not work on a 3-day one; split templates mostly just dictate frequency
Volume, intensity and frequency are the variables that matter; control them and the program's name does not matter
He dislikes separate volume and intensity days: intensity days get too many reps at intensities with poor form, and volume days get too much junk volume
Within each day mix ranges promoting high and moderate-high intensity; low-intensity training is a waste of time apart from myonuclear-overload-style work
Body part splits let evolving rep ranges express their full potential; push/pull/legs or full body can work but take more effort
Rep ranges are only intense if you push: a 3-6 range done at 80 percent is not very intense; he preaches training close to failure
